analysis.one_liner: Lets student borrowers erase student loans in bankruptcy like any other debt.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill 19–5, but it was never sent to the floor and died when that Congress ended without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strike the bankruptcy-law provision that makes student loans nearly impossible to erase, so a borrower who files for bankruptcy could discharge government, nonprofit, and private student loans just like credit card or medical debt. It was introduced with bipartisan support in May 2019 and cleared the House Judiciary Committee 19–5 in September 2020, but the committee never formally sent it to the full House, and no vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers whose debts have become unpayable. Under current law, a person in bankruptcy must prove "undue hardship" — a very high bar that varies by court — to erase student loans, while credit cards, medical bills, and almost everything else can be wiped clean. This bill would remove that special rule entirely, letting a bankruptcy judge discharge federal, nonprofit, and private student loans along with the rest of the filer's debts. It applies to bankruptcy cases filed after the law takes effect, not retroactively.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the special bankruptcy carve-out in section 523(a)(8) of the bankruptcy code, so student loans — federal, nonprofit, or private — can be discharged in bankruptcy like other unsecured debts.
Also lets borrowers discharge obligations to repay educational benefits, scholarships, or stipends, closing a gap beyond just loans.
Gives borrowers a genuine fresh start: instead of the uncertain 'undue hardship' test, the ordinary bankruptcy rules their creditors face would apply to student debt too.
Applies to bankruptcy cases filed on or after enactment, so it would not reopen old cases.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders whose loans become dischargeable. Private lenders like Sallie Mae/Navient would face higher risk on their student loans, since a share of borrowers would erase the debt in bankruptcy, which could mean higher interest rates or tighter credit for future student borrowers. The federal government would also lose money when taxpayers' federal loans are discharged, and loan servicers and debt collectors would lose the stream of payments and fees from distressed borrowers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private lenders and federal loan program

drawbacks.text: Taxpayers would absorb losses when federal student loans are discharged in bankruptcy, since the government's loan portfolio loses its special protection.
Private lenders would price in the new discharge risk, which could mean higher interest rates on student loans or less credit available to some borrowers, especially those with weaker credit.

Because the bill removes the protection completely rather than setting a fairer standard (for example, allowing discharge after a set number of years of good-faith repayment), borrowers who can pay but choose bankruptcy would qualify alongside those who genuinely cannot.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is real but narrow: it would matter most to the relatively small group of borrowers so distressed they actually file for bankruptcy, not the broad run of student debtors. The honest costs are taxpayer losses on discharged federal loans and the chance that private lenders charge more or lend less to future students. A supporter would accept that trade as the price of treating student debt like any other debt; a critic would note the bill does nothing for borrowers who need help but will never file for bankruptcy, and that a less blunt standard might have been easier to pass.

outcome.mechanism: The Judiciary Committee approved it 19–5 in September 2020, but the committee never formally reported the bill to the full House, so no floor vote ever happened before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on May 9, 2019 with 13 original cosponsors, including Republican Rep. John Katko, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
It sat in a Judiciary subcommittee for over a year before being discharged on September 14, 2020, meaning the subcommittee was pulled off the bill so the full committee could act.
On September 29, 2020, after two markup sessions, the Judiciary Committee voted 19–5 to order the bill reported with amendments — a strong, apparently bipartisan vote.

But ordering a bill reported is not the same as reporting it: the committee never took the final step of officially sending the bill to the House floor, and no further action appears before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing the bill.

The bill's sponsor, Jerrold Nadler, was himself the chairman of the Judiciary Committee during this period, so the committee that approved the bill was the one that let it lapse without filing the report.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders, loan servicers, and the federal loan program are better off, because the special bankruptcy protection that keeps student loans nearly impossible to erase survived unchanged. Distressed borrowers got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private lenders and the federal loan program

for.role: Chair, House Judiciary Committee; bill sponsor

for.role: House Republican from New York; lead Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: 19 House Judiciary Committee members
for.what_they_did: Voted 19–5 on September 29, 2020 to order the bill reported with amendments.

against.name: 5 House Judiciary Committee members
against.what_they_did: Voted no when the committee ordered the bill reported.

against.name: Private student lenders and servicers
against.what_they_did: The industry has long defended the special bankruptcy protection for student loans, which dates to 2005 legislation it backed, and has opposed repeal efforts like this one.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — 28 Democrats and 1 Republican cosponsor — and a 19–5 committee vote, but the party breakdown of that vote and of the 5 no votes is not in the record.

industries.note: Their loans would become dischargeable in bankruptcy, raising the risk that a share of balances is simply erased. Their gain under the status quo comes from a legal protection ordinary debts do not have, so their interest runs against borrowers here.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: A bankruptcy discharge ends their collections, fees, and recovery activity on the affected loans. The value of their contracts depends partly on loans being hard to escape.

Government-backed loans would be dischargeable, so taxpayers would absorb losses on some discharged balances — though borrowers who genuinely cannot pay gain the most. The program would also face pressure to price that risk into future lending.
